speaker: Will Guidara
title: Talking Unreasonable Hospitality, Culture, and Leadership with Will Guidara
question: In hospitality and retail operations, why do managers who worked their way up from frontline roles still lose their empathy advantage over time?
guest: Anyone who's ever been promoted through an organization can relate to this. I'll just use my industry to prove the point. When you're a busboy, you look at the world through the eyes of a busboy. When you become a server, one of your superpowers is you can see the world through the eyes of a busboy, but a couple seasons pass, and now you can't do it anymore. Now you only see the world through the eyes of a server. My dad would always have me journal my perspectives, so that later in life I could tap back into it and be a more enlightened manager to people, no matter what role they played.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Managers promoted from the floor lose their empathy edge mainly because the experience that produced it stops being current, while their new position actively pulls their attention elsewhere.

First, memory fades and distorts. People in a "cold" state consistently underestimate how physical fatigue, rude customers, and time pressure felt in the moment (the hot-cold empathy gap). Research by Rachel Ruttan and colleagues even found that people who have endured a hardship can be less compassionate toward those now struggling with it: "I coped, so can you."

Second, power changes perspective. Studies by Galinsky, Keltner, and others show that holding authority reduces perspective-taking and attention to subordinates' experience.

Third, the job changes what they see and are rewarded for. Their days fill with labor budgets, KPIs, and pressure from above, so they begin viewing staff through metrics and identifying with management.

Fourth, the frontline job itself moves on. New technology, scheduling systems, staffing levels, and customer behavior mean their knowledge describes a job that no longer exists, yet they remain confident in it.

The remedy is regular, real shifts on the floor and structured listening, not reliance on past experience.

models.answer:
Managers promoted from the floor lose their empathy advantage through a combination of psychological distortion, structural incentives, and operational drift. Paradoxically, having survived frontline hardship creates a "been-there" empathy gap: once removed from the visceral stress of service rushes and difficult guests, managers forget how exhausting those moments felt and treat their own past perseverance as proof that current staff should simply tough it out.

At the same time, promotion rewires daily accountability around labor percentages, sales targets, and shift coverage. Squeezed between corporate directives and chronic turnover, overloaded middle managers develop compassion fatigue and start experiencing employee struggles—burnout, illness, or scheduling conflicts—as operational friction rather than human needs. Positional authority further dulls perspective-taking while the frontline role keeps changing: leaner staffing models, omnichannel tasks, algorithmic scheduling, and sharper customer incivility mean the floor a manager remembers rarely matches today's reality, turning outdated memory into false certainty that they still understand the job.

Managers promoted from the frontline lose their empathy advantage primarily because their incentives, daily environment, and memory of the job steadily diverge from frontline reality. Once in management, they are evaluated on labor ratios, throughput, shrinkage, and compliance rather than peer solidarity, which trains them to view staff problems through the lens of cost and efficiency. At the same time, administrative work pulls them off the floor while staffing models, technology, and customer demands continue to evolve, leaving their mental model of frontline work outdated.

Psychological adaptation accelerates this drift. Trapped between corporate pressure from above and staff or customer frustrations from below, managers often develop emotional detachment to survive chronic understaffing and high turnover. Over time, survivorship bias also sets in: remembering their own early struggles as character-building rather than exhausting makes them less patient with current employees. Without deliberate effort to stay connected to the floor, structural pressure quietly replaces lived understanding.
